item.title: IMF urges exchange rate flexibility as RBI steps up rupee defence
item.description: The IMF urged Asian economies to allow exchange rates to absorb global shocks as the RBI steps up efforts to support the rupee amid oil price pressures and foreign outflows ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Foreign-exchange intervention offers limited benefits beyond the near term and currencies should be allowed to adjust to global shocks, a top International Monetary Fund official said. “Countries which allow exchange rates to move have benefited more,” Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, said at a press conference in Mumbai on Wednesday, responding to a question about Asian currencies. With economies facing a succession of global shocks, exchange rates should be allowed to absorb some of the pressure and act as the “first line of defense,” he said, without naming the Reserve Bank of India. Central banks across Asia are grappling with currency weakness as global shocks drive capital outflows and boost demand for dollars. Policymakers from Indonesia to Japan have deployed a mix of interest-rate increases and market intervention, testing how far authorities can resist depreciation without running down reserves or imposing greater costs on their economies. In India, the RBI is mounting its most forceful defense of the rupee since the 2013 taper tantrum. The currency has been among Asia’s worst performers this year, pressured by elevated oil prices and persistent foreign outflows from Indian stocks. The RBI this month rolled out a special window to meet dollar demand from state-run oil companies and a new tool requiring banks to park cash against certain foreign-exchange transactions. The moves followed its first interest-rate increase in nearly four years, as policymakers confront the risk that a weaker rupee and elevated crude could further stoke inflation. The IMF drew a distinction, however, between intervening in the currency market and measures designed to attract capital. Ranil Salgado, its senior resident representative for India, Bhutan and Maldives, described recent RBI steps to ease foreign inflows as broadly positive. “We think that is a good policy,” he said. The central bank has sought to bolster dollar supplies by easing rules for foreign borrowing and offering incentives to attract foreign-currency deposits from overseas Indians. Those measures have brought in billions of dollars, helping cushion pressure on the rupee without relying solely on the RBI’s reserves. Salgado also noted that the RBI’s stated policy is to curb excessive currency volatility rather than defend a particular exchange-rate level.

item.title: Rate cuts off table as RBI MPC flags inflation risks, two dissent on stance
item.description: RBI MPC minutes show members concerned about broadening inflation, with two dissenting on the shift to calibrated tightening despite unanimous support for a 25-basis-point rate hike ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: With headline inflation projected to touch the upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent in the third quarter of the current financial year, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has signalled that rate cuts are off the table in the near term. Minutes of its October meeting, released on Wednesday, show members increasingly concerned about inflation spreading beyond food and fuel. While all six members voted for a 25-basis-point hike in the repo rate to 5.50 per cent, Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh opposed the shift in the monetary policy stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. The minutes of the October 5-7 meeting show that the change in stance was intended to signal a shift in the policy outlook. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said it conveyed that rate cuts were unlikely in the near term, leaving a rate hike or a pause as the possible next moves. The duration and extent of any tightening cycle would depend on underlying inflation, the spread of price pressures and the second-round effects of the supply shock, he said. “I feel it is appropriate to change the stance to calibrated tightening, essentially signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term,” said Malhotra.  The case for raising rates rested on a change in the inflation outlook. Headline consumer price index (CPI) inflation rose to 4.8 per cent in August from 4.5 per cent in July, while core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent. The MPC projected inflation at 5.2 per cent for 2026-27, with the third quarter expected to see it touch 6 per cent, the upper end of the RBI’s tolerance band. While members agreed on the need for a rate hike, they differed on the extent to which inflation had become broad-based and persistent. Saugata Bhattacharya said price pressures were getting entrenched, pointing to wholesale input prices rising close to 9 per cent and the pass-through of higher costs to consumers. He also questioned whether monetary conditions were too accommodative, arguing that current and projected real interest rates were not consistent with price stability. “Too rapid a policy rate adjustment risks constricting growth and hence growth-led capital flows,” said Bhattacharya. Indranil Bhattacharyya called for the MPC to move away from a cautiousness bias and act pre-emptively. He cited sharp increases in weighted median and trimmed-mean inflation, along with higher inflation expectations among urban and rural households. “Inflation outlook merits greater attention, given supply side pressures from crude and food prices are unlikely to relent quickly,” said Bhattacharyya. Singh also pointed to signs of inflation broadening, citing the RBI’s September household survey, which showed the median three-month-ahead inflation expectation rising to 9.9 per cent. He warned that the real repo rate could turn negative under the projected inflation trajectory. However, he favoured gradual and moderate rate increases rather than keeping rates high for an extended period. A tightening stance, he argued, could signal a prolonged rate-hike cycle and undermine the growth-supportive measures taken in recent months. “Expectations of significant rate increases can undermine demand not only in interest rate-sensitive sectors but also drag on recent momentum in private investment,” singh said. Kumar, however, maintained that inflation was largely driven by supply-side factors, with little evidence of overheating or a broad-based increase in prices. He argued that the neutral stance remained appropriate amid geopolitical and trade uncertainties. “While inflation is driven largely by supply-side factors and does not show any signs of overheating of the economy nor of generalisation, it is important to manage inflationary expectations,” Kumar said. Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta, who proposed the change in stance, said inflation was largely driven by external supply shocks and showed limited signs of becoming entrenched. However, she argued that the MPC could not wait for definitive evidence of second-round effects, given the lag with which monetary policy affects prices. Referring to the post-pandemic inflation-targeting period, Gupta said the MPC had acted whenever inflation reached the tolerance limits, helping preserve the credibility of the framework. She added that a further increase in the policy rate might be needed, depending on incoming data on inflation, its spread across the basket and second-round effects. “With projections indicating the likelihood of headline inflation hitting the upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent, one may not want to wait for more definitive evidence of generalisation, and instead be mindful of the fact that monetary policy works with a lag,” said Gupta. The minutes also reflect concerns about the risks of excessive tightening. Bhattacharya said domestic financial conditions had already tightened significantly, reducing the need for large policy actions. The pace of further rate increases would need to be calibrated carefully, he said, warning that rapid adjustments could constrain growth and weaken the growth-led capital flows that India relies on. He also flagged vulnerabilities in India’s balance of payments amid tight global financial conditions, noting the importance of maintaining an interest-rate differential with G7 economies to attract debt flows. Global uncertainties featured in the committee’s assessment, including renewed tensions in West Asia, volatile crude oil prices and the US Federal Reserve’s 25-basis-point rate hike in September, amid elevated global bond yields. The MPC’s next meeting is scheduled for December 2-4. By then, members will have two more inflation readings and a clearer assessment of how much of the supply shock is feeding through to domestic prices.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military

Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defence drone missions against Russia

Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 8:21 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Elon Musk last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.   Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.   Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defence drone missions against Russia.   Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week, according to the report, which added the two had also discussed the matter prior to the decision to throttle Starlink.

Reuters had reported exclusively that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House. Also Read

Tesla shareholders to vote on Musk's re-election, $158 bn pay on Dec 3

Ukraine suspects US restricting intelligence sharing on Russian Attacks

Putin proposes summit with Trump, Xi Jinping to discuss Ukraine deal

Elon Musk says he will gift SpaceX shares to 'every kid in America'

Diesel deal aimed to keep peace talks with Russia going, says Trump

Trump said last week he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access, while Musk said any limits on speed or Starship use were decided by the US military or the president.   Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskky's relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskky.   Zelenskky, who is in Oslo in a bid to repair US relations, said on Tuesday he discussed issues including "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored" with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday Washington had not pulled back Ukraine's ability to access Starling's satellite network, but signaled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
